video_title: The latest scandals from OpenAI, Anthropic & Google are pretty bad | Rob Wiblin
transcript: We need more people holding AI companies  to account when they do bad things. That means staff inside companies objecting  loudly and clearly — and sometimes even quitting   and speaking up in public. It means investigative  journalists digging up information the public has   a right to know. It means highly informed people  explaining exactly what companies are doing,   and why it’s wrong. And it means  advocates across all sorts of media   making sure their misbehaviour is  getting the attention it deserves. The track record of that work  is actually pretty remarkable   for the modest amount of effort that  has gone into it. That’s in part because   many people in the companies legitimately  want to do the right thing. And in part it’s   because companies are scared their staff are  going to conclude that they’re the bad guys,   and that this will make it harder for them  to retain and hire the talent they need. The capacity to hold AI companies to  account for their actions is becoming   more important as events are moving  faster and faster — there often just   won’t be time to wait for governments to  take action or pass legislation. We also   need the option to bring down the immediate  hammer of fierce public and expert outrage. In the last few weeks, if we needed it,   we got yet more evidence about how  important that capacity is likely to be.   Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google DeepMind all had  serious scandals that warranted giving them hell. Today I’m going to lay out what each did wrong,   and the capacity we need to build to be able  to hold these organisations’ feet to the fire. First: Anthropic. Anthropic markets themselves as the good guys:  the ones who take the power of AI seriously,   build it carefully, and actively  want regulation to reduce the risks. So I was pretty disappointed to  learn that they’d been quietly   shopping around a draft federal AI bill  that would make it extremely hard for   anyone to stop a frontier AI company  doing something extremely dangerous. Under their proposed bill, the only way the  federal government could halt model training   is for the Commerce Secretary to personally  sign off on a detailed case and take it to a   single federal court in DC. The government  would have to establish an imminent risk,   backed by a specific explanation of how the  model could cause catastrophic harm and when.   They’d have to prove that nothing  less restrictive would work.   And the judge would decide each case from  scratch, with no deference to the regulator. On top of that, stop orders would expire after  45 days, and any renewal would require proving   the whole case again. And on top of that,  it’s unclear whether a credible 10% chance   of causing human extinction next year would be  sufficient to get a stop order under these rules,   because it may or may not qualify as “present  or impending,” the language used in the bill. Now, it’s true the White House would still keep  existing tools like export controls that it can   try to appropriate to tackle AI risk, even though  they weren’t designed for that purpose at all.   But the point of this legislation is to create  the dedicated brake for catastrophic AI risk in   particular — and the brake it’s creating  seems designed to be very hard to pull. At the same time, the proposed legislation would   bar US states from requiring AI companies  to publish their safety plans and tests,   or get independent evaluations, or report  incidents. And so it would retroactively kill   most of the flagship AI laws passed  by California, Illinois, and New York. And most importantly, the draft lists  another thing for US states to lose:   the power to halt an AI model because it poses  an imminent catastrophic risk “by statute,   regulation, order, judicial  decree, or other action.” In the leaked text, the clause isn’t  actually connected to the part of the   bill that does the preempting, so as  written, states would keep that power.   But it’s hard to see why the clause  is in there unless the draft is meant   to take that power away from states, at  least once the federal process existed. And if it were completed the  way that seems designed to work,   then even if everyone in California’s government  thought Anthropic was about to do something with   an unreleased model that might literally kill  everyone in the state, they couldn’t pass a law   or seek a statutory court order to stop it.  They’d be left hoping and praying that the   Commerce Secretary would go to a court in  DC and clear that very high bar I described. This is kind of weird coming from a company  whose CEO puts the chance of AI going “really,   really badly” at 25%, and he wrote in September   that recursive self-improvement “must  be pursued very carefully, if at all.” But on the other hand, given the fights they’ve  had with the Trump administration this year,   I can absolutely understand  why Anthropic doesn’t want   to empower the federal executive with  enormous discretion over these issues. A number of people in the Trump administration  have been extremely hostile to the company,   and seem basically out to get it in whatever way  they can. Those folks would likely try to use any   discretion the White House had to extract all  sorts of political concessions from Anthropic,   while doing nothing at all about  actually dangerous research practices. So I get it. But if you’re really worried about the Trump  administration or a future rogue US president,   the natural solution is just to leave  that power in the hands of US states   like California for the time being, and  help a number of relevant states to pass   bills focused on catastrophic AI risk  that would cover all the major players. Just as an aside, for Anthropic,  which is generally worried about   extreme concentration of power driven by AI,  I think there’s a case for avoiding federal   preemption and continuing to regulate AI  at the state level for some time to come. The most dangerous setup for extreme concentration  of power in human hands is to put control over AI   companies into the same hands that already control  the US military and the US intelligence services.   That’s just a very potent and threatening  combination, that’s very open to abuse — much   more so than if this responsibility is  just left with the California government. But alternatively, if you mostly want to  keep federal preemption, a different and   very simple way to improve on Anthropic’s draft  would have been to allow state attorneys general   to petition the DC court, as well as the Secretary  of Commerce. That avoids a really obvious single   point of failure, and feels just clearly better  for anyone who takes risks from AI very seriously. But Anthropic’s approach ties California’s hands,  it ties the hands of state attorneys general,   and it ties the hands of state courts. Which  means in practice it would likely lead to an   outcome where Anthropic, for the most part, was  just left to decide for itself whether to stop   model training or using a model because the  risk of loss of control had gotten too high. I’m sincerely kind of confused about what the  thinking is here. Because even if Anthropic   believed it had completely solved alignment and so  it posed no danger to anyone — which it doesn’t,   but let’s imagine — surely even then at some point  other more reckless AI companies would need to be   stopped from blasting ahead with recursive  self-improvement in a really incompetent way   and thereby generating intolerable risks. By  taking states out of the picture and giving   exclusive responsibility to the Department of  Commerce, this bill would make that harder to do. So I think this legislation is really  wrong-headed, and it’s worrying that Anthropic was   pushing it privately in a way that made it very  hard for insiders or outsiders to object to it. Naturally Anthropic got absolutely  blasted for this online.   The head of federal affairs put out  a long defence. And Dario conceded it   was among the things they could have handled  better, and put it down to communication. But I think the core disagreement  isn’t just about communication. Anthropic says it’s going to rewrite the  preemption language, but as of recording it only   seems to be saying it’ll let states set standards  for evaluators, and regulate the existence of kill   switches — not allow states to retain any ability  to halt model training or deployment themselves. The single highest-stakes issue in AI regulation  is who gets to stop AI companies engaging in   really reckless R&D when going ahead risks  actual human extinction. And for now, Anthropic’s   answer appears to still be: one agency, one  court, and only once the threat is imminent. In my view it shouldn’t be  up to a handful of people at   one AI company and the Secretary of  Commerce and a single federal judge   to decide whether or not to roll  the dice with all our lives. If you’re inside Anthropic,   please speak up and say this is a bad  proposal the company shouldn’t be pushing.   If you keep the pressure up, it’s likely the  policy team will see reason and propose something   that strikes a more reasonable balance between  the different competing considerations at play. How about OpenAI? Well, as you might have heard, OpenAI  recently fired three safety researchers:   Tomek Korbak, Mikita Balesni, and Jasmine Wang. The reasons they say they were given for their  firings were really weak and different for each   person, even though all three were fired  in simultaneous 2pm meetings. That made   the justifications seem probably pretextual — and  indeed OpenAI later said there was a bigger breach   of trust, though it wouldn’t say exactly what.  That left it unclear what the actual motivation   or possible breach of trust was. Why did OpenAI  want any of these people gone in the first place? Well, new reporting from the  Wall Street Journal suggests   the firings originated from a leak investigation. On September 1, The Information reported  that OpenAI’s new model, Astra, used a   technique called “looped transformers.” This  was something OpenAI didn’t want anyone to know. According to Korbak and Balesni, OpenAI’s  investigators eventually became suspicious   that the leak about looped transformers had gotten  to The Information via an outside researcher, Ryan   Greenblatt, who they had both been speaking with  as part of their work. OpenAI insisted on seeing   the Signal chats that they had with Greenblatt.  But they both used disappearing messages with him,   which meant they couldn’t prove they hadn’t  messaged him about the looped transformers. To be clear, the three researchers and  Greenblatt all strongly deny leaking anything,   and as far as we know there’s  no proof that they did. But up until now, OpenAI hasn’t  revealed anything else that would   explain the sudden and simultaneous firings.  So it seems fairly likely that what happened   is the company concluded that plausibly either  Korbak or Balesni could have been the leaker,   and decided it had to get rid  of them on that suspicion alone. Jasmine Wang was also asked about the leak,  so she was potentially a suspect as well,   even though she didn’t have any disappearing  messages. The thing is, all three of them had   been vocal about the importance of keeping  AI chain of thought monitorable, so probably   the idea was that they would be particularly  likely to disapprove of looped transformers. Just to back up and give a little context:  looped transformers increase the amount of   computation a model can perform before writing  down what it’s thinking on the chain of thought.   That makes it harder to notice if  it’s doing things we don’t want,   which is why researchers across the industry  had warned that they were potentially the start   of a slippery slope towards models  that couldn’t be monitored at all. That’s why, when the story broke, there was such  a big backlash, and one former OpenAI researcher   said the company seemed to be violating “one of  the few redlines that exist in the industry.” Now, if leadership at OpenAI really believes  that using looped transformers is fine — and   they claim to have evidence that it is —  then it’s natural enough for any company   to want to fire staff it’s convinced  have leaked trade secrets to the press. However, a few things. As far as we  know, the evidence that any one of   these three leaked that information is  somewhere between weak and nonexistent. First, using disappearing messages to discuss  anything and everything is totally normal in   the tech industry, and the AI world in  particular, so by itself that simply   isn’t grounds for much suspicion at all.  Applying that standard consistently,   almost everyone at the company could be  suspected of a leak and fired, from the CEO down. Second, The Information has been breaking stories  about AI companies’ internal plans for years, from   details of OpenAI’s secret “Strawberry” model to  the terms of Google’s Pentagon contract this year.   It clearly just has many sources  in and around these companies,   including investors and former staff,  and probably a lot of stuff also   leaks out through conversations  overheard at parties and so on. So there’s no particular reason to assume people  worried about safety were the source here;   this could just be another piece of juicy gossip  that reached The Information one way or another. Third, if it were leaked by someone  who objected to looped transformers,   there could easily be 100 or 200 or even more  OpenAI staff who thought it was a really bad idea.   Almost 400 OpenAI staff signed a petition  earlier this year backing a push to slow AI   down for safety reasons. And adding  recurrent depth to models is among   the most controversial research directions in  AI, something a lot of people think is misguided. Fourth, if you’re willing to admit a personal  character judgement — I really think Greenblatt   in particular is unlikely to have been involved in  this leak. That was also the immediate reaction of   a lot of other people in the AI world: “Ryan  Greenblatt is meant to have leaked this?   No, that doesn’t sound right.” Leaking  stuff to the press is just not his vibe,   and it’s in total conflict with the  research work he actually wants to do.   However this information got to The Information,  I would bet my bottom dollar it wasn’t him. So the case that any of them is  responsible is not particularly compelling.   The leak investigators have maybe just  made a mistake or done a poor job here. And on the other side of the ledger, you’ve  got clear, terrible negative impacts. They lost three great AI researchers focused on   what the company says is one of its  top safety and alignment problems. The company created the impression that they fire  staff who visibly speak up about the safety issues   they’re concerned about, so OpenAI is going  to have a harder time getting candid opinions   from staff in future. In fact, I think that  probably wasn’t their complaint with these three,   but it’s how it looked to basically everyone  when their firings were first announced. They also made it seem risky for staff  to speak to anyone outside of OpenAI,   even when they’re doing it for legitimate work  purposes and doing nothing wrong whatsoever. And by concluding that one of these three  is responsible for the leak on the basis   of almost no evidence, they probably let the  actual leaker go permanently unidentified. So unless there’s non-public evidence yet  to come to light, which is indeed possible,   I would guess that these firings were  a mistake — not just by my lights,   but even just by the lights  of OpenAI’s senior management. Staff inside the company should say clearly  that the tradeoffs OpenAI has struck here are   unacceptable. They’re simply bad for the company,  bad for its culture, and bad for its staff. Sadly, OpenAI is not too  likely to rehire these three,   even if they are fully cleared of  the leaking charge at some point.   But the more internal and external grief  OpenAI gets for this behaviour, the less   likely they are to shoot from the hip and make  a similar regrettable decision next time around. Alright, let’s talk Google DeepMind. According to Google DeepMind staff who spoke  to the BBC in mid-October, their UK employment   contracts bar them from publicly criticising  anything Google does, for the rest of their lives. That sounds kind of crazy. It’s one thing to say staff shouldn’t be  publicly laying into you while working for you,   or shouldn’t criticise you based on confidential  information they know through their work.   But it’s very different and very  abnormal to say that they can’t   criticise anything an enormous entity  like Google does so long as they live. This anti-criticism provision came up because  it’s creating problems for ex-Googlers who want to   criticise the company’s decision to sell AI to the  US Department of War for any use the Department of   War itself deems lawful — something which has  upset a lot of staff and led a number to quit. I was really quite surprised to learn about this,  because two years ago there was this massive   firestorm about OpenAI using non-disparagement  agreements to muzzle its employees. At the time, much of the compensation OpenAI  staff were getting was in the form of shares   and equity in the company — shares they had  to wait to sell. And it turned out that OpenAI   was forcing all staff who left the firm to  sign an agreement to never criticise OpenAI,   or it would confiscate all the shares in the  company that they’d earned while working there,   costing that person millions or perhaps even  tens of millions of dollars. Furthermore,   this no-disparagement provision itself had  to remain completely secret — if you allowed   anyone to learn of its existence, that alone  might lead you to lose all of your equity. When this came out, thanks in large part to  former guests of the show Daniel Kokotajlo and   Kelsey Piper, the company was lambasted in the  press, staff were furious, and the company had   to rip up those conditions, while they tried to  pretend it was all a big misunderstanding. Kelsey   Piper’s reporting left it unambiguous that it  was approved by executives at the highest level. As a result of all of this, Anthropic had  to admit that it also had non-disparagement   terms in its severance agreements, terms  which it also then promised to remove. And now it seems like this entire time  Google DeepMind has also had the same thing. Unless I’m misunderstanding, thousands  of incoming staff must have seen this   term in their employment contracts, and it  doesn’t come with a secrecy requirement.   I really don’t get how it could have  been kept under wraps for so long. That’s   either incredible loyalty or incredible  passivity from Google DeepMind staff. Now, to be fair, there’s two ways the  Google DeepMind contracts are less bad   than what OpenAI was doing. Firstly, it comes  in a contract at the start of your employment,   rather than the end — so you could read  it and refuse to work there, I guess.   Plus OpenAI’s threat to confiscate millions of  dollars in equity like that is just much more   severe than anything courts would plausibly impose  on a past employee for criticising Google. In   practice, Google would be unlikely to bring a case  anyway, because it’s just going to look so bad. But still — the threat of ending up  in litigation is a huge deterrent   for an ordinary person to criticise an  extremely powerful company like Google. In my view, Google DeepMind staff should  speak up and say clearly that the company   ought to remove or rewrite these sweeping  anti-criticism clauses, so staff who leave   Google can enjoy some of the same freedom as  staff who move on from OpenAI or Anthropic.   Their opinions about AI are just as  valuable for the public to be hearing. Now, those three stories are all pretty  bad. But of course Anthropic, OpenAI,   and Google — these are huge companies that  make large numbers of decisions every week, and   every week companies do good  things as well as bad ones. For example, I saw last week that  Anthropic and OpenAI are each giving   £100 million in compute credits to a new AI  Biosecurity Lab here in London. That’s cool. Anthropic published a study where they red-teamed  the safety monitors they use with their AI agents.   It showed that more than half of sophisticated  attacks got through, and they then released   the tools they used so others can test  and fix their monitors the same way. And OpenAI revealed that when one of its models  found its way onto the open internet during   training back in September, it paused frontier  training for almost two weeks, had its most   capable models try to break out of the sandbox,  and they fixed what they found before restarting. It’s all good to see. And the fact that  these companies are not only willing to   stop doing bad things, but often willing to  do many more good things as well — that makes   it even more valuable to influence  the choices they decide to make. So with that in mind, what do we need to  most effectively drive AI companies to   be better actors? Let me break down how  different people can contribute to the   effort — first people inside the AI companies,  and then all of the rest of us outside of them. People inside AI companies really have very  disproportionate influence, and it’s urgently   time for them to exercise it. That’s because  it may well become possible to automate most   of what they do in the next few years, at which  point they just aren’t going to be so needed,   and much of their leverage will be gone. So  if now isn’t the moment to use your voice to   influence the company you work at, you really have  to ask yourself what on Earth you’re waiting for. Some people are nervous about staff being more  vocal inside AI companies, because they’re worried   that this could lead to people being fired or  sidelined, and later decisions being made by the   more reckless people who remain. It’s a legitimate  worry. Though others argue that most staff can   actually do more good outside AI companies than  inside them anyway, so it’s fine if they leave. Either way, I think you can become a more vocal  AI company insider either with a view to staying,   or with a view to leaving. Both are totally fine. How about if your top priority  is to remain where you are? Well, as always, you will know better than me  about your company and your situation and your   team, so exercise your own best judgement.  But here’s the default approach I’ll take. Simply speak up in public Slack channels  that lots of your colleagues can see,   explaining carefully and reasonably why you  oppose particular decisions the company is making,   on the merits. Act with integrity and assume  good faith from the people you’re talking to.   Just give your actual reasons clearly, calmly,  and intelligently. Keep bringing the conversation   back to the central issue, and stay focused on  just the handful of most consequential issues,   rather than objecting to everything and  generally being difficult. And certainly   be open to being persuaded to change your mind  if people make really good arguments in reply. OpenAI and Anthropic say that they encourage  staff to dissent and provide input. And I think   for the most part — despite everything I’ve  said — they’re sincere about that. So take   them at their word, and test the proposition  that they would like intelligent pushback.   And treat this work as one of the most important  parts of your job rather than just a distraction. Keep in mind, if you identify a mistake or  problem ahead of time, that can easily enhance   your credibility and decisions going forward.  And if you’re the first person to speak up   about something, it makes it a lot easier for  other colleagues who may also have the same   reservations, but are more shy or more junior  — it makes it easier for them to do the same. What about at the other extreme,   if you’re completely happy to leave the  company you’re working at currently? Well, if it were me, I’d still just start  by explaining carefully and reasonably to   your colleagues in public channels why you  disapprove of things the company is doing,   and why you think they’re harmful. Again,  making a good argument, acting with integrity,   and passing the ideological Turing test is simply  more likely to persuade the people who matter. But if you consistently raise serious  and legitimate objections and don’t   get good answers, or find that your  worries aren’t addressed in some way,   you can escalate to saying that these  experiences have led you to question the   company’s judgement or strategy, and as a result  you’re considering taking your talents elsewhere. And then if that doesn’t bear fruit, resign  and post a thorough, thoughtful explanation   to the company of why you’ve decided to leave,  and encourage others to think for themselves.   Then, once you’re out, announce your  departure publicly and clearly lay   out your reasons for doing so in a way that  will resonate with your former colleagues,   while also making sense to the general  public and politicians who are reading.   Then go get a job elsewhere — there are many  places that desperately need your skills. Should you actively plan to leave your job at  an AI company? I don’t really have a strong   take either way. It’s going to depend on the  details, and who you are, and what you want to do. Of course, there’s a lot of important safety and  alignment work people can do inside AI companies,   and a lot of key decisions that are really made  there. But because they can pay the most and   have incredible headhunting teams, companies  have comparatively less difficulty hiring. So by default I’d expect that a marginal  person choosing between different paths   could likely expect to have  more impact at an AISI, or METR,   or Redwood, or LawZero, or any  of a number of other places. So if you don’t feel like it’s working  out, or you think your company is simply   pursuing the wrong high-level strategy,  you should consider going elsewhere. It’s clear that many people who have departed AI  companies have gone on to have incredible impact   outside of them — maybe more impact than they  had in them. Geoffrey Hinton, Beth Barnes, Jacob   Coxon, David Robinson, Helen Toner, and Daniel  Kokotajlo all jump to mind as possible cases. So don’t be intimidated into silence. If we  reach the end and you haven’t made a fuss   about something, you’ve almost certainly left  some possible positive impact on the table. What about the great majority of  people who are outside the companies? Well, there’s a particular sort of agitation that  seems to have already borne significant fruit,   which is work by sophisticated actors who  have a lot of context on what’s going on.   Sometimes these efforts win hearts and  minds inside the companies. Other times they   effectively strong-arm a company into doing things  it didn’t want to do, but now it kind of has to. Probably the most significant example here  is the “Not For Private Gain” campaign   against OpenAI’s plans to sideline its  nonprofit owner and its charitable purpose.   The number of people involved was tiny, but their  effort, along with the necessary attention from   the state attorneys general and the broader  coalition of campaigners with other concerns,   forced through very significant  changes to the plan. The end result was the OpenAI Foundation  got a stake worth perhaps $75 billion   more than what originally seemed likely.   And its Safety and Security Committee now  has a locked-in power to impose decisions   on a wide range of safety and security issues —  a power that could ultimately matter enormously. Another success of sophisticated advocacy  was the Right to Warn campaign back in 2024,   which was led by ex-company staff, and likely   evolved into the significant whistleblower  protections provided by California’s SB 53. Another win is that over the last year, OpenAI  has taken a lot of flak for publicly saying   it’s in favour of sensible AI regulation,  while in the background invisibly lobbying   to sabotage and block any regulation that it  could, at both the state and federal level.   That took careful work to uncover,  make easy to understand, and publicise.   And it appears to have contributed to OpenAI  gradually shifting its stance, and now   actually supporting rather than opposing  AI regulations along the lines of SB 53. The same effort probably contributed  to Greg Brockman, OpenAI’s president,   ending his donations to the notorious  super PAC Leading the Future,   which was doing all sorts of shady stuff while  trying to prevent any regulation of AI whatsoever. And I already mentioned earlier the case  where a handful of people who left OpenAI   managed to get both OpenAI and Anthropic to   put an end to the non-disparagement  agreements that were gagging staff. OK, so what do we need to scale up in order  to radically increase the outside pressure   on companies? Frankly, it’s quite an open field,  with a lot of things that aren’t getting owned by   anyone and so they’re not getting done. But let  me just throw out some ideas to give you leads. The first cluster is more  specialised, and involves   accessing, processing, and explaining information. Firstly, there’s digging into and  exposing company misbehaviour,   or failures, or weaknesses — either as a  journalist or an outside technical expert.   The Tarbell Fellowship is a great example —  they train and fund AI-focused journalists.   There’s also the newly formed Nightingale  Collective, which recently uncovered AI   swarms in the wild and publicised their findings,  and got a lot of media coverage of the problem.   And you’ve also got the Midas Project, which  seems to specifically try to uncover the most   embarrassing AI company chicanery and hypocrisy  that they possibly can. It’s quite entertaining. Second, there’s assisting AI company staff to  exercise their legally sanctioned whistleblower   rights, which obviously one has to do  carefully and ideally with legal support.   A few groups in that space include the  AI Whistleblower Initiative, Psst.org,   and Larry Lessig. Obviously, if you’re planning  to become a legally protected whistleblower,   visit their websites on a personal  device, not your work one. Third, there’s work to help journalists,  politicians, regulators, and other significant   actors understand what’s going on and why it’s  bad, so they can do more accurate reporting, or   make better use of congressional hearings, or not  be fooled by company statements, or whatever else.   This is more important than you might think.  The amount of context you need to fully grasp   what AI companies are up to and why is really  substantial at this point. For people who are new   to this topic it can be very confusing — doubly  so if someone is actively trying to confuse you. A great organisation here is Legal  Advocates for Safe Science and Technology,   which did essential legal analysis  for the Not For Private Gain campaign.   I interviewed their founder  Tyler Whitmer back at the time. Fourth, there’s producing content that is actually  persuasive to staff in these companies, and   speaking with them personally, so they understand  and are motivated to push to change course.   Ideally this requires really appreciating the  constraints they face, and why they’re doing   what they’re doing now, and what they can  realistically be convinced to do instead.   A project along these lines is Guidelight  AI Standards, which pushes companies   to make concrete improvements to  frontier AI development practices. Among other things, they have technical analysis  of what AI companies are and aren’t doing, which   finds, for instance, that at least back in August  OpenAI had a much better containment plan than   Anthropic did. They say that’s because: “We have  found no evidence that Anthropic has a containment   response plan, or has any plans to adopt one.” If  that’s correct, rather than a misunderstanding,   maybe some Anthropic staff who are listening  can encourage the company to work on that. The second big cluster is trying to reach  a broad audience outside the AI and tech   industries, to stimulate mass outrage when  massively outrageous things are going on.   There’s obviously a huge range  of things in this category,   and I feel like I know less about it —  but again, I’ll throw out some thoughts. One approach would be to disproportionately reach  politicians and people who work in politics,   whether in DC or at the state level. And another  would just be to try to reach as many people as   you can with massive coverage through social  media, TV, newspapers, podcasts, and so on. Ideally we’ll just have way more informed and  credible people who the press knows to call when   they want to discuss an emerging AI issue, because  they’ve helped with their reporting in the past,   or they’ve been great on TV before, or they  consistently put out good analysis online. A group I’m really impressed with that does  some of all of this is Encode AI, which has   been involved in all sorts of campaigns. They  both provide detailed analysis for legislators,   and they’re very effective at reaching a  wider public audience as well. Nathan Calvin,   who you saw criticising Anthropic’s proposed  legislation and getting a response from the   company — he works at Encode, and we interviewed  their founder Sneha Revanur a few months ago. There are many Pause AI and Control  AI organisations that are also in this   broad category, and they might be well  placed to take advantage of this issue   becoming much more important and salient  to the public over the next few years.   Last year, Pause AI UK managed to get 60 members  of the UK Parliament to sign an open letter   criticising Google DeepMind for probably  violating its own AI safety commitments. Now, if you have a knack for directing attention  to particular topics by producing engaging   content or getting “earned media,” that could  absolutely be your biggest opportunity for impact.   I’m thinking stunts, memes, jokes, billboards,  clips, viral videos and text posts, and so on.   It takes a particular kind of person to succeed  at this, and it’s a weirdly valuable skill in   the modern world — one that in most cases  should be cultivated rather than squandered. You might start by racking up views on  YouTube or Instagram or TikTok or Facebook,   or wherever you have a relative advantage.  And then convert that into also getting   your ideas covered on TV, cable news,  magazines, newspapers, podcasts, and so on. This work is naturally open to a wider range of  people who don’t have any existing involvement in   the tech industry — that’s one of the attractive  things about it. But I would be remiss if I didn’t   say that people who used to work at AI companies  are really unusually credible to the public on   the topic of whether an AI company is behaving  badly, and if so, what it should do differently. If you’re an ex-company employee and you can  stomach it, get professional comms advice and   training, and prepare yourself to be available  to go on TV, or do interviews with newspapers,   or write op-eds, when these topics flare up to  massive public attention — as they’re absolutely   certain to do again. Unfortunately, a lot of  opportunities for earned media are being dropped,   or not used very effectively, because many  potential spokespeople aren’t honing their   communication skills, or getting connected, or  even just putting themselves out there at all. Alright. Bottom line is that AI  companies love to talk a big talk   about how safe and responsible and great  they are, and how much we can trust them.   But their track record is extremely mixed. Every  week they do a combination of good and bad things,   and reasonably often they do  some quite outrageous things.   I gave three examples from the last few weeks,  but I could do the same almost any week now. Fortunately, experience over the last few years  shows it’s not a hopeless case. Staff inside   the companies can speak up and make the case for  the company to do better, and they do often get   their way, partially if not completely. People  outside companies can organise to turn up the   heat by persuading staff inside the company, and  persuading politicians, and persuading regulators,   and persuading voters and the general  public, that what is going on is not OK. Fairly few people have adopted this strategy so  far, especially people with enormous context,   who have typically gone into more traditional AI  policy, governance, research, or technical roles.   But the skilled people who have taken on this work   have managed to have a very  outsized influence so far. The more we collectively practice,  and find ways to get coordinated,   the more we’ll be able to quickly respond to  events and exert a powerful effect on events   when the stakes are much higher in coming years. And on that note, I’ll speak with you again soon.

transcript_segments.text: We need more people holding AI companies  to account when they do bad things.
That means staff inside companies objecting  loudly and clearly — and sometimes even quitting
and speaking up in public. It means investigative  journalists digging up information the public has
a right to know. It means highly informed people  explaining exactly what companies are doing,
and why it’s wrong. And it means  advocates across all sorts of media
making sure their misbehaviour is  getting the attention it deserves.
The track record of that work  is actually pretty remarkable
for the modest amount of effort that  has gone into it. That’s in part because
many people in the companies legitimately  want to do the right thing. And in part it’s
because companies are scared their staff are  going to conclude that they’re the bad guys,
and that this will make it harder for them  to retain and hire the talent they need.
The capacity to hold AI companies to  account for their actions is becoming
more important as events are moving  faster and faster — there often just
won’t be time to wait for governments to  take action or pass legislation. We also
need the option to bring down the immediate  hammer of fierce public and expert outrage.
In the last few weeks, if we needed it,
we got yet more evidence about how  important that capacity is likely to be.
Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google DeepMind all had  serious scandals that warranted giving them hell.
Today I’m going to lay out what each did wrong,
and the capacity we need to build to be able  to hold these organisations’ feet to the fire.
First: Anthropic.
Anthropic markets themselves as the good guys:  the ones who take the power of AI seriously,
build it carefully, and actively  want regulation to reduce the risks.
So I was pretty disappointed to  learn that they’d been quietly
shopping around a draft federal AI bill  that would make it extremely hard for
anyone to stop a frontier AI company  doing something extremely dangerous.
Under their proposed bill, the only way the  federal government could halt model training
is for the Commerce Secretary to personally  sign off on a detailed case and take it to a
single federal court in DC. The government  would have to establish an imminent risk,
backed by a specific explanation of how the  model could cause catastrophic harm and when.
They’d have to prove that nothing  less restrictive would work.
And the judge would decide each case from  scratch, with no deference to the regulator.
On top of that, stop orders would expire after  45 days, and any renewal would require proving
the whole case again. And on top of that,  it’s unclear whether a credible 10% chance
of causing human extinction next year would be  sufficient to get a stop order under these rules,
because it may or may not qualify as “present  or impending,” the language used in the bill.
Now, it’s true the White House would still keep  existing tools like export controls that it can
try to appropriate to tackle AI risk, even though  they weren’t designed for that purpose at all.
But the point of this legislation is to create  the dedicated brake for catastrophic AI risk in
particular — and the brake it’s creating  seems designed to be very hard to pull.
At the same time, the proposed legislation would
bar US states from requiring AI companies  to publish their safety plans and tests,
or get independent evaluations, or report  incidents. And so it would retroactively kill
most of the flagship AI laws passed  by California, Illinois, and New York.
And most importantly, the draft lists  another thing for US states to lose:
the power to halt an AI model because it poses  an imminent catastrophic risk “by statute,
regulation, order, judicial  decree, or other action.”
In the leaked text, the clause isn’t  actually connected to the part of the
bill that does the preempting, so as  written, states would keep that power.
But it’s hard to see why the clause  is in there unless the draft is meant
to take that power away from states, at  least once the federal process existed.
And if it were completed the  way that seems designed to work,
then even if everyone in California’s government  thought Anthropic was about to do something with
an unreleased model that might literally kill  everyone in the state, they couldn’t pass a law
or seek a statutory court order to stop it.  They’d be left hoping and praying that the
Commerce Secretary would go to a court in  DC and clear that very high bar I described.
This is kind of weird coming from a company  whose CEO puts the chance of AI going “really,
really badly” at 25%, and he wrote in September
that recursive self-improvement “must  be pursued very carefully, if at all.”
But on the other hand, given the fights they’ve  had with the Trump administration this year,
I can absolutely understand  why Anthropic doesn’t want
to empower the federal executive with  enormous discretion over these issues.
A number of people in the Trump administration  have been extremely hostile to the company,
and seem basically out to get it in whatever way  they can. Those folks would likely try to use any
discretion the White House had to extract all  sorts of political concessions from Anthropic,
while doing nothing at all about  actually dangerous research practices.
So I get it.
But if you’re really worried about the Trump  administration or a future rogue US president,
the natural solution is just to leave  that power in the hands of US states
like California for the time being, and  help a number of relevant states to pass
bills focused on catastrophic AI risk  that would cover all the major players.
Just as an aside, for Anthropic,  which is generally worried about
extreme concentration of power driven by AI,  I think there’s a case for avoiding federal
preemption and continuing to regulate AI  at the state level for some time to come.
The most dangerous setup for extreme concentration  of power in human hands is to put control over AI
companies into the same hands that already control  the US military and the US intelligence services.
That’s just a very potent and threatening  combination, that’s very open to abuse — much
more so than if this responsibility is  just left with the California government.
But alternatively, if you mostly want to  keep federal preemption, a different and
very simple way to improve on Anthropic’s draft  would have been to allow state attorneys general
to petition the DC court, as well as the Secretary  of Commerce. That avoids a really obvious single
point of failure, and feels just clearly better  for anyone who takes risks from AI very seriously.
But Anthropic’s approach ties California’s hands,  it ties the hands of state attorneys general,
and it ties the hands of state courts. Which  means in practice it would likely lead to an
outcome where Anthropic, for the most part, was  just left to decide for itself whether to stop
model training or using a model because the  risk of loss of control had gotten too high.
I’m sincerely kind of confused about what the  thinking is here. Because even if Anthropic
believed it had completely solved alignment and so  it posed no danger to anyone — which it doesn’t,
but let’s imagine — surely even then at some point  other more reckless AI companies would need to be
stopped from blasting ahead with recursive  self-improvement in a really incompetent way
and thereby generating intolerable risks. By  taking states out of the picture and giving
exclusive responsibility to the Department of  Commerce, this bill would make that harder to do.
So I think this legislation is really  wrong-headed, and it’s worrying that Anthropic was
pushing it privately in a way that made it very  hard for insiders or outsiders to object to it.
Naturally Anthropic got absolutely  blasted for this online.
The head of federal affairs put out  a long defence. And Dario conceded it
was among the things they could have handled  better, and put it down to communication.
But I think the core disagreement  isn’t just about communication.
Anthropic says it’s going to rewrite the  preemption language, but as of recording it only
seems to be saying it’ll let states set standards  for evaluators, and regulate the existence of kill
switches — not allow states to retain any ability  to halt model training or deployment themselves.
The single highest-stakes issue in AI regulation  is who gets to stop AI companies engaging in
really reckless R&D when going ahead risks  actual human extinction. And for now, Anthropic’s
answer appears to still be: one agency, one  court, and only once the threat is imminent.
In my view it shouldn’t be  up to a handful of people at
one AI company and the Secretary of  Commerce and a single federal judge
to decide whether or not to roll  the dice with all our lives.
If you’re inside Anthropic,
please speak up and say this is a bad  proposal the company shouldn’t be pushing.
If you keep the pressure up, it’s likely the  policy team will see reason and propose something
that strikes a more reasonable balance between  the different competing considerations at play.
How about OpenAI?
Well, as you might have heard, OpenAI  recently fired three safety researchers:
Tomek Korbak, Mikita Balesni, and Jasmine Wang.
The reasons they say they were given for their  firings were really weak and different for each
person, even though all three were fired  in simultaneous 2pm meetings. That made
the justifications seem probably pretextual — and  indeed OpenAI later said there was a bigger breach
of trust, though it wouldn’t say exactly what.  That left it unclear what the actual motivation
or possible breach of trust was. Why did OpenAI  want any of these people gone in the first place?
Well, new reporting from the  Wall Street Journal suggests
the firings originated from a leak investigation.
On September 1, The Information reported  that OpenAI’s new model, Astra, used a
technique called “looped transformers.” This  was something OpenAI didn’t want anyone to know.
According to Korbak and Balesni, OpenAI’s  investigators eventually became suspicious
that the leak about looped transformers had gotten  to The Information via an outside researcher, Ryan
Greenblatt, who they had both been speaking with  as part of their work. OpenAI insisted on seeing
the Signal chats that they had with Greenblatt.  But they both used disappearing messages with him,
which meant they couldn’t prove they hadn’t  messaged him about the looped transformers.
To be clear, the three researchers and  Greenblatt all strongly deny leaking anything,
and as far as we know there’s  no proof that they did.
But up until now, OpenAI hasn’t  revealed anything else that would
explain the sudden and simultaneous firings.  So it seems fairly likely that what happened
is the company concluded that plausibly either  Korbak or Balesni could have been the leaker,
and decided it had to get rid  of them on that suspicion alone.
Jasmine Wang was also asked about the leak,  so she was potentially a suspect as well,
even though she didn’t have any disappearing  messages. The thing is, all three of them had
been vocal about the importance of keeping  AI chain of thought monitorable, so probably
the idea was that they would be particularly  likely to disapprove of looped transformers.
Just to back up and give a little context:  looped transformers increase the amount of
computation a model can perform before writing  down what it’s thinking on the chain of thought.
That makes it harder to notice if  it’s doing things we don’t want,
which is why researchers across the industry  had warned that they were potentially the start
of a slippery slope towards models  that couldn’t be monitored at all.
That’s why, when the story broke, there was such  a big backlash, and one former OpenAI researcher
said the company seemed to be violating “one of  the few redlines that exist in the industry.”
Now, if leadership at OpenAI really believes  that using looped transformers is fine — and
they claim to have evidence that it is —  then it’s natural enough for any company
to want to fire staff it’s convinced  have leaked trade secrets to the press.
However, a few things. As far as we  know, the evidence that any one of
these three leaked that information is  somewhere between weak and nonexistent.
First, using disappearing messages to discuss  anything and everything is totally normal in
the tech industry, and the AI world in  particular, so by itself that simply
isn’t grounds for much suspicion at all.  Applying that standard consistently,
almost everyone at the company could be  suspected of a leak and fired, from the CEO down.
Second, The Information has been breaking stories  about AI companies’ internal plans for years, from
details of OpenAI’s secret “Strawberry” model to  the terms of Google’s Pentagon contract this year.
It clearly just has many sources  in and around these companies,
including investors and former staff,  and probably a lot of stuff also
leaks out through conversations  overheard at parties and so on.
So there’s no particular reason to assume people  worried about safety were the source here;
this could just be another piece of juicy gossip  that reached The Information one way or another.
Third, if it were leaked by someone  who objected to looped transformers,
there could easily be 100 or 200 or even more  OpenAI staff who thought it was a really bad idea.
Almost 400 OpenAI staff signed a petition  earlier this year backing a push to slow AI
down for safety reasons. And adding  recurrent depth to models is among
the most controversial research directions in  AI, something a lot of people think is misguided.
Fourth, if you’re willing to admit a personal  character judgement — I really think Greenblatt
in particular is unlikely to have been involved in  this leak. That was also the immediate reaction of
a lot of other people in the AI world: “Ryan  Greenblatt is meant to have leaked this?
No, that doesn’t sound right.” Leaking  stuff to the press is just not his vibe,
and it’s in total conflict with the  research work he actually wants to do.
However this information got to The Information,  I would bet my bottom dollar it wasn’t him.
So the case that any of them is  responsible is not particularly compelling.
The leak investigators have maybe just  made a mistake or done a poor job here.
And on the other side of the ledger, you’ve  got clear, terrible negative impacts.
They lost three great AI researchers focused on
what the company says is one of its  top safety and alignment problems.
The company created the impression that they fire  staff who visibly speak up about the safety issues
they’re concerned about, so OpenAI is going  to have a harder time getting candid opinions
from staff in future. In fact, I think that  probably wasn’t their complaint with these three,
but it’s how it looked to basically everyone  when their firings were first announced.
They also made it seem risky for staff  to speak to anyone outside of OpenAI,
even when they’re doing it for legitimate work  purposes and doing nothing wrong whatsoever.
And by concluding that one of these three  is responsible for the leak on the basis
of almost no evidence, they probably let the  actual leaker go permanently unidentified.
So unless there’s non-public evidence yet  to come to light, which is indeed possible,
I would guess that these firings were  a mistake — not just by my lights,
but even just by the lights  of OpenAI’s senior management.
Staff inside the company should say clearly  that the tradeoffs OpenAI has struck here are
unacceptable. They’re simply bad for the company,  bad for its culture, and bad for its staff.
Sadly, OpenAI is not too  likely to rehire these three,
even if they are fully cleared of  the leaking charge at some point.
But the more internal and external grief  OpenAI gets for this behaviour, the less
likely they are to shoot from the hip and make  a similar regrettable decision next time around.
Alright, let’s talk Google DeepMind.
According to Google DeepMind staff who spoke  to the BBC in mid-October, their UK employment
contracts bar them from publicly criticising  anything Google does, for the rest of their lives.
That sounds kind of crazy.
It’s one thing to say staff shouldn’t be  publicly laying into you while working for you,
or shouldn’t criticise you based on confidential  information they know through their work.
But it’s very different and very  abnormal to say that they can’t
criticise anything an enormous entity  like Google does so long as they live.
This anti-criticism provision came up because  it’s creating problems for ex-Googlers who want to
criticise the company’s decision to sell AI to the  US Department of War for any use the Department of
War itself deems lawful — something which has  upset a lot of staff and led a number to quit.
I was really quite surprised to learn about this,  because two years ago there was this massive
firestorm about OpenAI using non-disparagement  agreements to muzzle its employees.
At the time, much of the compensation OpenAI  staff were getting was in the form of shares
and equity in the company — shares they had  to wait to sell. And it turned out that OpenAI
was forcing all staff who left the firm to  sign an agreement to never criticise OpenAI,
or it would confiscate all the shares in the  company that they’d earned while working there,
costing that person millions or perhaps even  tens of millions of dollars. Furthermore,
this no-disparagement provision itself had  to remain completely secret — if you allowed
anyone to learn of its existence, that alone  might lead you to lose all of your equity.
When this came out, thanks in large part to  former guests of the show Daniel Kokotajlo and
Kelsey Piper, the company was lambasted in the  press, staff were furious, and the company had
to rip up those conditions, while they tried to  pretend it was all a big misunderstanding. Kelsey
Piper’s reporting left it unambiguous that it  was approved by executives at the highest level.
As a result of all of this, Anthropic had  to admit that it also had non-disparagement
terms in its severance agreements, terms  which it also then promised to remove.
And now it seems like this entire time  Google DeepMind has also had the same thing.
Unless I’m misunderstanding, thousands  of incoming staff must have seen this
term in their employment contracts, and it  doesn’t come with a secrecy requirement.
I really don’t get how it could have  been kept under wraps for so long. That’s
either incredible loyalty or incredible  passivity from Google DeepMind staff.
Now, to be fair, there’s two ways the  Google DeepMind contracts are less bad
than what OpenAI was doing. Firstly, it comes  in a contract at the start of your employment,
rather than the end — so you could read  it and refuse to work there, I guess.
Plus OpenAI’s threat to confiscate millions of  dollars in equity like that is just much more
severe than anything courts would plausibly impose  on a past employee for criticising Google. In
practice, Google would be unlikely to bring a case  anyway, because it’s just going to look so bad.
But still — the threat of ending up  in litigation is a huge deterrent
for an ordinary person to criticise an  extremely powerful company like Google.
In my view, Google DeepMind staff should  speak up and say clearly that the company
ought to remove or rewrite these sweeping  anti-criticism clauses, so staff who leave
Google can enjoy some of the same freedom as  staff who move on from OpenAI or Anthropic.
Their opinions about AI are just as  valuable for the public to be hearing.
Now, those three stories are all pretty  bad. But of course Anthropic, OpenAI,
and Google — these are huge companies that  make large numbers of decisions every week, and
every week companies do good  things as well as bad ones.
For example, I saw last week that  Anthropic and OpenAI are each giving
£100 million in compute credits to a new AI  Biosecurity Lab here in London. That’s cool.
Anthropic published a study where they red-teamed  the safety monitors they use with their AI agents.
It showed that more than half of sophisticated  attacks got through, and they then released
the tools they used so others can test  and fix their monitors the same way.
And OpenAI revealed that when one of its models  found its way onto the open internet during
training back in September, it paused frontier  training for almost two weeks, had its most
capable models try to break out of the sandbox,  and they fixed what they found before restarting.
It’s all good to see. And the fact that  these companies are not only willing to
stop doing bad things, but often willing to  do many more good things as well — that makes
it even more valuable to influence  the choices they decide to make.
So with that in mind, what do we need to  most effectively drive AI companies to
be better actors? Let me break down how  different people can contribute to the
effort — first people inside the AI companies,  and then all of the rest of us outside of them.
People inside AI companies really have very  disproportionate influence, and it’s urgently
time for them to exercise it. That’s because  it may well become possible to automate most
of what they do in the next few years, at which  point they just aren’t going to be so needed,
and much of their leverage will be gone. So  if now isn’t the moment to use your voice to
influence the company you work at, you really have  to ask yourself what on Earth you’re waiting for.
Some people are nervous about staff being more  vocal inside AI companies, because they’re worried
that this could lead to people being fired or  sidelined, and later decisions being made by the
more reckless people who remain. It’s a legitimate  worry. Though others argue that most staff can
actually do more good outside AI companies than  inside them anyway, so it’s fine if they leave.
Either way, I think you can become a more vocal  AI company insider either with a view to staying,
or with a view to leaving. Both are totally fine.
How about if your top priority  is to remain where you are?
Well, as always, you will know better than me  about your company and your situation and your
team, so exercise your own best judgement.  But here’s the default approach I’ll take.
Simply speak up in public Slack channels  that lots of your colleagues can see,
explaining carefully and reasonably why you  oppose particular decisions the company is making,
on the merits. Act with integrity and assume  good faith from the people you’re talking to.
Just give your actual reasons clearly, calmly,  and intelligently. Keep bringing the conversation
back to the central issue, and stay focused on  just the handful of most consequential issues,
rather than objecting to everything and  generally being difficult. And certainly
be open to being persuaded to change your mind  if people make really good arguments in reply.
OpenAI and Anthropic say that they encourage  staff to dissent and provide input. And I think
for the most part — despite everything I’ve  said — they’re sincere about that. So take
them at their word, and test the proposition  that they would like intelligent pushback.
And treat this work as one of the most important  parts of your job rather than just a distraction.
Keep in mind, if you identify a mistake or  problem ahead of time, that can easily enhance
your credibility and decisions going forward.  And if you’re the first person to speak up
about something, it makes it a lot easier for  other colleagues who may also have the same
reservations, but are more shy or more junior  — it makes it easier for them to do the same.
What about at the other extreme,
if you’re completely happy to leave the  company you’re working at currently?
Well, if it were me, I’d still just start  by explaining carefully and reasonably to
your colleagues in public channels why you  disapprove of things the company is doing,
and why you think they’re harmful. Again,  making a good argument, acting with integrity,
and passing the ideological Turing test is simply  more likely to persuade the people who matter.
But if you consistently raise serious  and legitimate objections and don’t
get good answers, or find that your  worries aren’t addressed in some way,
you can escalate to saying that these  experiences have led you to question the
company’s judgement or strategy, and as a result  you’re considering taking your talents elsewhere.
And then if that doesn’t bear fruit, resign  and post a thorough, thoughtful explanation
to the company of why you’ve decided to leave,  and encourage others to think for themselves.
Then, once you’re out, announce your  departure publicly and clearly lay
out your reasons for doing so in a way that  will resonate with your former colleagues,
while also making sense to the general  public and politicians who are reading.
Then go get a job elsewhere — there are many  places that desperately need your skills.
Should you actively plan to leave your job at  an AI company? I don’t really have a strong
take either way. It’s going to depend on the  details, and who you are, and what you want to do.
Of course, there’s a lot of important safety and  alignment work people can do inside AI companies,
and a lot of key decisions that are really made  there. But because they can pay the most and
have incredible headhunting teams, companies  have comparatively less difficulty hiring.
So by default I’d expect that a marginal  person choosing between different paths
could likely expect to have  more impact at an AISI, or METR,
or Redwood, or LawZero, or any  of a number of other places.
So if you don’t feel like it’s working  out, or you think your company is simply
pursuing the wrong high-level strategy,  you should consider going elsewhere.
It’s clear that many people who have departed AI  companies have gone on to have incredible impact
outside of them — maybe more impact than they  had in them. Geoffrey Hinton, Beth Barnes, Jacob
Coxon, David Robinson, Helen Toner, and Daniel  Kokotajlo all jump to mind as possible cases.
So don’t be intimidated into silence. If we  reach the end and you haven’t made a fuss
about something, you’ve almost certainly left  some possible positive impact on the table.
What about the great majority of  people who are outside the companies?
Well, there’s a particular sort of agitation that  seems to have already borne significant fruit,
which is work by sophisticated actors who  have a lot of context on what’s going on.
Sometimes these efforts win hearts and  minds inside the companies. Other times they
effectively strong-arm a company into doing things  it didn’t want to do, but now it kind of has to.
Probably the most significant example here  is the “Not For Private Gain” campaign
against OpenAI’s plans to sideline its  nonprofit owner and its charitable purpose.
The number of people involved was tiny, but their  effort, along with the necessary attention from
the state attorneys general and the broader  coalition of campaigners with other concerns,
forced through very significant  changes to the plan.
The end result was the OpenAI Foundation  got a stake worth perhaps $75 billion
more than what originally seemed likely.
And its Safety and Security Committee now  has a locked-in power to impose decisions
on a wide range of safety and security issues —  a power that could ultimately matter enormously.
Another success of sophisticated advocacy  was the Right to Warn campaign back in 2024,
which was led by ex-company staff, and likely
evolved into the significant whistleblower  protections provided by California’s SB 53.
Another win is that over the last year, OpenAI  has taken a lot of flak for publicly saying
it’s in favour of sensible AI regulation,  while in the background invisibly lobbying
to sabotage and block any regulation that it  could, at both the state and federal level.
That took careful work to uncover,  make easy to understand, and publicise.
And it appears to have contributed to OpenAI  gradually shifting its stance, and now
actually supporting rather than opposing  AI regulations along the lines of SB 53.
The same effort probably contributed  to Greg Brockman, OpenAI’s president,
ending his donations to the notorious  super PAC Leading the Future,
which was doing all sorts of shady stuff while  trying to prevent any regulation of AI whatsoever.
And I already mentioned earlier the case  where a handful of people who left OpenAI
managed to get both OpenAI and Anthropic to
put an end to the non-disparagement  agreements that were gagging staff.
OK, so what do we need to scale up in order  to radically increase the outside pressure
on companies? Frankly, it’s quite an open field,  with a lot of things that aren’t getting owned by
anyone and so they’re not getting done. But let  me just throw out some ideas to give you leads.
The first cluster is more  specialised, and involves
accessing, processing, and explaining information.
Firstly, there’s digging into and  exposing company misbehaviour,
or failures, or weaknesses — either as a  journalist or an outside technical expert.
The Tarbell Fellowship is a great example —  they train and fund AI-focused journalists.
There’s also the newly formed Nightingale  Collective, which recently uncovered AI
swarms in the wild and publicised their findings,  and got a lot of media coverage of the problem.
And you’ve also got the Midas Project, which  seems to specifically try to uncover the most
embarrassing AI company chicanery and hypocrisy  that they possibly can. It’s quite entertaining.
Second, there’s assisting AI company staff to  exercise their legally sanctioned whistleblower
rights, which obviously one has to do  carefully and ideally with legal support.
A few groups in that space include the  AI Whistleblower Initiative, Psst.org,
and Larry Lessig. Obviously, if you’re planning  to become a legally protected whistleblower,
visit their websites on a personal  device, not your work one.
Third, there’s work to help journalists,  politicians, regulators, and other significant
actors understand what’s going on and why it’s  bad, so they can do more accurate reporting, or
make better use of congressional hearings, or not  be fooled by company statements, or whatever else.
This is more important than you might think.  The amount of context you need to fully grasp
what AI companies are up to and why is really  substantial at this point. For people who are new
to this topic it can be very confusing — doubly  so if someone is actively trying to confuse you.
A great organisation here is Legal  Advocates for Safe Science and Technology,
which did essential legal analysis  for the Not For Private Gain campaign.
I interviewed their founder  Tyler Whitmer back at the time.
Fourth, there’s producing content that is actually  persuasive to staff in these companies, and
speaking with them personally, so they understand  and are motivated to push to change course.
Ideally this requires really appreciating the  constraints they face, and why they’re doing
what they’re doing now, and what they can  realistically be convinced to do instead.
A project along these lines is Guidelight  AI Standards, which pushes companies
to make concrete improvements to  frontier AI development practices.
Among other things, they have technical analysis  of what AI companies are and aren’t doing, which
finds, for instance, that at least back in August  OpenAI had a much better containment plan than
Anthropic did. They say that’s because: “We have  found no evidence that Anthropic has a containment
response plan, or has any plans to adopt one.” If  that’s correct, rather than a misunderstanding,
maybe some Anthropic staff who are listening  can encourage the company to work on that.
The second big cluster is trying to reach  a broad audience outside the AI and tech
industries, to stimulate mass outrage when  massively outrageous things are going on.
There’s obviously a huge range  of things in this category,
and I feel like I know less about it —  but again, I’ll throw out some thoughts.
One approach would be to disproportionately reach  politicians and people who work in politics,
whether in DC or at the state level. And another  would just be to try to reach as many people as
you can with massive coverage through social  media, TV, newspapers, podcasts, and so on.
Ideally we’ll just have way more informed and  credible people who the press knows to call when
they want to discuss an emerging AI issue, because  they’ve helped with their reporting in the past,
or they’ve been great on TV before, or they  consistently put out good analysis online.
A group I’m really impressed with that does  some of all of this is Encode AI, which has
been involved in all sorts of campaigns. They  both provide detailed analysis for legislators,
and they’re very effective at reaching a  wider public audience as well. Nathan Calvin,
who you saw criticising Anthropic’s proposed  legislation and getting a response from the
company — he works at Encode, and we interviewed  their founder Sneha Revanur a few months ago.
There are many Pause AI and Control  AI organisations that are also in this
broad category, and they might be well  placed to take advantage of this issue
becoming much more important and salient  to the public over the next few years.
Last year, Pause AI UK managed to get 60 members  of the UK Parliament to sign an open letter
criticising Google DeepMind for probably  violating its own AI safety commitments.
Now, if you have a knack for directing attention  to particular topics by producing engaging
content or getting “earned media,” that could  absolutely be your biggest opportunity for impact.
I’m thinking stunts, memes, jokes, billboards,  clips, viral videos and text posts, and so on.
It takes a particular kind of person to succeed  at this, and it’s a weirdly valuable skill in
the modern world — one that in most cases  should be cultivated rather than squandered.
You might start by racking up views on  YouTube or Instagram or TikTok or Facebook,
or wherever you have a relative advantage.  And then convert that into also getting
your ideas covered on TV, cable news,  magazines, newspapers, podcasts, and so on.
This work is naturally open to a wider range of  people who don’t have any existing involvement in
the tech industry — that’s one of the attractive  things about it. But I would be remiss if I didn’t
say that people who used to work at AI companies  are really unusually credible to the public on
the topic of whether an AI company is behaving  badly, and if so, what it should do differently.
If you’re an ex-company employee and you can  stomach it, get professional comms advice and
training, and prepare yourself to be available  to go on TV, or do interviews with newspapers,
or write op-eds, when these topics flare up to  massive public attention — as they’re absolutely
certain to do again. Unfortunately, a lot of  opportunities for earned media are being dropped,
or not used very effectively, because many  potential spokespeople aren’t honing their
communication skills, or getting connected, or  even just putting themselves out there at all.
Alright. Bottom line is that AI  companies love to talk a big talk
about how safe and responsible and great  they are, and how much we can trust them.
But their track record is extremely mixed. Every  week they do a combination of good and bad things,
and reasonably often they do  some quite outrageous things.
I gave three examples from the last few weeks,  but I could do the same almost any week now.
Fortunately, experience over the last few years  shows it’s not a hopeless case. Staff inside
the companies can speak up and make the case for  the company to do better, and they do often get
their way, partially if not completely. People  outside companies can organise to turn up the
heat by persuading staff inside the company, and  persuading politicians, and persuading regulators,
and persuading voters and the general  public, that what is going on is not OK.
Fairly few people have adopted this strategy so  far, especially people with enormous context,
who have typically gone into more traditional AI  policy, governance, research, or technical roles.
But the skilled people who have taken on this work
have managed to have a very  outsized influence so far.
The more we collectively practice,  and find ways to get coordinated,
the more we’ll be able to quickly respond to  events and exert a powerful effect on events
when the stakes are much higher in coming years.
And on that note, I’ll speak with you again soon.
